Because Missus Mallard was afflicted with heart trouble, great care was taken to break the news of her husbands death to her as gently as possible. <break time="0.8s" /> It was her sister Josephine who told her, in broken sentences and veiled hints that revealed the truth while half hiding it. <break time="0.8s" /> Her husbands friend Richards was there too, because he had been in the newspaper office when news of the railroad disaster arrived. <break time="0.8s" /> Brently Mallards name had led the list of the killed, and Richards, who wanted to be sure, had checked it with a second telegram. <break time="0.8s" /> He had then hurried to the Mallards house, hoping to arrive before any less careful and less tender friend could bring the sad message. <break time="0.8s" /> She did not hear the story as many women have heard the same, with a frozen inability to accept what it meant. <break time="0.8s" /> She wept at once, with sudden, wild abandonment, in her sisters arms, and her whole body shook with the force of her tears. <break time="0.8s" /> When the storm of grief had spent itself, she went away to her room alone, and she would have no one follow her.

There stood, facing the open window, a comfortable, roomy armchair, into which she sank with a physical exhaustion that seemed to reach into her soul. <break time="0.8s" /> Through the window she could see, in the open square before her house, trees whose tops were trembling with the new spring life. <break time="0.8s" /> The delicious breath of rain was in the air, and in the street below a peddler was crying his wares to passers by. <break time="0.8s" /> Faintly she could hear someone singing a distant song, and countless sparrows were twittering in the eaves of the houses. <break time="0.8s" /> In the west facing her window, the clouds had piled one above another, but patches of blue sky were showing here and there through them. <break time="0.8s" /> She sat with her head thrown back upon the cushion of the chair, quite motionless, except when a sob came up into her throat. <break time="0.8s" /> She was like a child who has cried itself to sleep and still sobs in its dreams, long after the crying has stopped. <break time="0.8s" /> She was young, with a fair, calm face, whose lines showed a long habit of holding back her feelings and also a certain strength. <break time="0.8s" /> But now there was a dull stare in her eyes, which were fixed far away on one of those patches of blue sky.
